messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai, a 54-year-old combat pilot of Oceanian descent, presented for therapy at the urging of his wife, concerned by the profound changes she had observed in him since an incident two years prior. Married for thirty years, Kai had always been a man of quiet strength and composure, but the man who sat before him now was a stranger. The precipitating event had been a catastrophic hydraulic failure during a routine combat patrol. Kai, a veteran F-18 pilot, had wrestled with the dying aircraft, manually overriding systems for a harrowing emergency landing in hostile territory. He’d barely managed to extricate himself from the mangled cockpit before the jet became a fireball, the roar and heat permanently seared into his memory. He sustained physical injuries that healed, but the internal damage proved more insidious.

In the months that followed, Kai found himself increasingly distant from his former self. He confided that he now felt like he didn't know himself anymore, as if the man who had loved flying and shared an easy camaraderie with his fellow pilots had simply vanished. This profound sense of identity loss was coupled with a bleak conviction: he believed he had permanently changed for the worse, an irreparable shift in his core being. The joy he once found in his family and his passion for the skies seemed muted, replaced by a dull ache, leading him to fear he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. He saw himself as irrevocably broken, a shell of his former self.

This deep-seated belief that he was fundamentally damaged, that something within him had been permanently altered for the worse, fueled a pervasive and exhausting vigilance. Because he felt so profoundly changed and vulnerable, his internal landscape demanded a constant external alertness, leading him to feel perpetually on guard. Even inside his own home, a place that had always been his sanctuary, Kai felt perpetually on guard, unable to truly relax. His wife noticed him scanning rooms, his eyes darting to windows, his posture rigid even during quiet evenings. This pervasive hypervigilance wasn't limited to his home; it extended into every aspect of his life. When out with his wife at their favorite restaurant, Kai found himself instinctively identifying escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, mentally mapping exits and potential threats, making it impossible to truly engage in conversation or enjoy the meal.

His professional life, too, was touched by this shift. While he continued to fly, his colleagues noted a new intensity, a quiet watchfulness that went beyond the disciplined focus of a combat pilot. What used to be a professional necessity had morphed into an all-consuming personal burden. He would spend hours after missions meticulously re-checking systems, poring over schematics, driven by an unshakeable feeling that he had to be superalert or watchful or on guard at all times, lest another catastrophe strike. His wife missed the easygoing husband who once laughed readily and shared stories from the squadron. Now, he seemed trapped in a silent battle, constantly scanning, constantly bracing.

Kai finally sought help because the exhaustion was becoming unbearable, and he could no longer ignore the growing chasm between himself and his wife. He confessed to feeling trapped by this constant vigilance, haunted by the belief that his former self was lost forever, and terrified that he would spend the rest of his life unable to experience the genuine joy and connection he once knew. He hoped therapy might offer a path back to himself, or at least a way to live with the stranger he had become.
